title: Scheduler policy options brainstorm (mixed short/long prompts)
content:
Context / why this doc exists
- We’re seeing p95 tail spikes for “interactive / short” traffic when co-scheduled with prefill-heavy long-context requests.
- Goal for prototype: reduce p95/p99 for short/interactive without tanking throughput, and without starving long.
- This is a brainstorming doc of policy options + knobs. Not a commitment.

Glossary / mental model
- “Short request” ~= small prompt prefill + typical streaming decode. Often latency sensitive.
- “Long request” ~= long prompt/context window, high prefill cost. Often batch/summarization, can be throughput oriented but still may have SLAs.
- Prefill vs decode: prefill cost tends to dominate for long prompts; decode can be long-running but is incremental.
- Continuous batching: changes how “service time” is experienced; batches can mix classes and create priority inversion if not careful.

Assumptions / constraints
- We can classify requests at enqueue-time with a cheap heuristic (tokens, predicted prefill cost, tier hints).
- We can adjust scheduling at microbatch boundaries (or “dispatch opportunities”). We cannot reliably preempt an in-flight GPU kernel.
- We want stable behavior under bursty arrivals; avoid oscillations (queue flipping, thrash) and avoid pathological batching.
- Must be feature-flagged and easy to disable.

Evaluation criteria (for all options)
- Latency: p50/p95/p99 end-to-end + separate “queue wait” vs “service time”.
- Tail breakdown: fraction of tail attributable to queue wait.
- Throughput: tokens/sec and request/sec, and GPU utilization.
- Fairness: long requests max wait bound or at least bounded starvation probability.
- Predictability: stable under burst; does not amplify microbatching artifacts.
- Complexity: implementation risk, observability required, and tuning burden.

Option A: FIFO (baseline)
Summary
- Single queue; always dispatch oldest eligible item (plus any existing batching logic).

Pros
- Simple; stable; minimal tuning.
- Easy to reason about and debug.
- Typically good throughput if batching works well.

Cons
- Bad for mixed workloads: one long prefill at head-of-line can inflate wait for many short requests.
- Under burst + long prompts, p95 for short tends to track long prefill “windows”.
- Doesn’t give us a lever to enforce “interactive” SLOs.

Knobs
- Existing batching knobs only (max batch size, max batch latency, etc.).

Notes
- FIFO is our “control” for benchmarking and canary.

Option B: Two-queue strict priority (short queue always served first)
Summary
- Maintain two queues: SHORT and LONG.
- On each dispatch opportunity: if SHORT non-empty, take from SHORT; else take from LONG.

Pros
- Biggest immediate p95 win for short (in many queueing systems).
- Straightforward to implement.
- Easy to explain externally (“interactive prioritized”).

Cons / risks
- Starvation risk for long (worst-case unbounded wait if short arrival rate stays high).
- Can harm throughput if LONG requests are better batch partners for GPU saturation (e.g., long prefill batches efficient), but strict priority keeps them from forming.
- Can create burst oscillations: short bursts drain, then long backlog, then short burst again.
- “Priority inversion” can still happen if batching mixes classes or a long prefill gets batched in a way that blocks short work (depends on dispatch semantics).

Knobs / parameter ideas
- short_threshold_tokens: e.g., prompt_tokens <= 256 or <= 512.
- long_threshold_tokens: prompt_tokens >= 1k/2k (leave middle as “medium” or classify via prefill prediction).
- short_queue_max_depth / admission control: avoid infinite short backlog if upstream overload.
- Batch formation rules:
  - prohibit mixing short+long in same prefill batch (strong isolation, but maybe throughput hit)
  - allow mixing decode tokens but not prefill (if we can separate phases)

Observability needed
- Per-class queue depth + wait time histograms.
- Starvation detector: long wait time p95/p99, max wait, and “time since last long dispatch”.

Option C: Two-queue priority with fairness window (aka “short-first, but serve long periodically”)
Summary
- Still two queues.
- Prefer SHORT, but enforce a fairness rule:
  - Serve at least 1 LONG every N dispatches, or
  - If LONG has waited > W ms, force a LONG dispatch, or
  - Use credit-based budgeting between classes.

Pros
- Retains most of the short p95 gains, while bounding long starvation.
- The “max wait” rule is intuitive and SRE-friendly (“long shouldn’t wait more than X”).
- Moderate implementation complexity.

Cons / risks
- Tuning required (N, W). Wrong knobs can either:
  - reintroduce tail for short (if too many long injections), or
  - still starve long under heavy short load (if too lenient).
- Interacts with batching: a forced long dispatch might start a big prefill batch at a bad time.
- Need careful definition of “dispatch opportunity” (per batch? per request?) to make the bound meaningful.

Knobs / parameter ideas
- fairness_window_dispatches (N): e.g., after 8 short batches, do 1 long batch.
- max_long_wait_ms (W): e.g., 250ms, 500ms, 1000ms depending on tier.
- max_short_burst_ms: allow serving short exclusively but only for a time budget.
- batch_isolation_mode:
  - strict: no mixing short+long in prefill batches
  - soft: mixing allowed if long predicted prefill cost below threshold
- “aging” factor: when long is waiting, its priority ramps up gradually instead of hard cutoff.

Fairness bound formulation options
- Hard max-wait bound (best for SRE): if any long item waited > W, dispatch long next.
- Soft bound (smoother): probability/weight of long increases with wait time.

What I think is the “prototype sweet spot”
- Two-queue + max_long_wait_ms + “serve long at least every N dispatches” guard.
- Keep mixing rules conservative initially to avoid priority inversion/regressions.

Option D: Weighted Fair Queueing / Deficit Round Robin (token-based fairness)
Summary
- Maintain separate queues per class (SHORT/LONG, maybe more).
- Allocate service share via weights. DRR is practical:
  - Each class gets a quantum of “credit” periodically.
  - A class can dispatch if it has enough credit; credit spent based on estimated cost.

Pros
- Explicit trade-off between latency and throughput; stable under sustained mixed load.
- Good story for multi-tenant future (could extend to per-customer-tier queues).
- Avoids strict starvation and can be made work-conserving.

Cons / risks
- Hard part: define “cost” for GPU inference.
  - prompt tokens? predicted prefill ms? predicted total tokens? observed rolling EWMA?
  - Wrong cost model yields unpredictable behavior and can be gamed.
- More complex to debug; requires better metrics.
- Needs guardrails to maintain short p95 (WFQ can still give short poor tail if long is constantly entitled to share).

Cost model candidates
- cost = prompt_tokens (prefill proxy)
- cost = predicted_prefill_ms (if we can predict)
- cost = prompt_tokens + alpha * expected_decode_tokens
- cost = observed_prefill_ms EWMA per route/model + prompt_tokens scaling

Knobs / parameter ideas
- weight_short : weight_long (e.g., 3:1, 5:1)
- quantum units:
  - tokens
  - ms (if prediction exists)
- min_short_share: ensure short gets at least X% of dispatch opportunities.
- max_long_burst: cap consecutive long dispatches even if it has credit.

Observability needed
- Credits over time per class.
- “Effective service share” metrics: % of GPU time or tokens allocated per class.
- Debug traces: why a class was skipped (no credit, empty, throttled).

Option E: SRPT-like heuristic (Shortest Remaining Processing Time approximation)
Summary
- Always select the request with smallest predicted remaining service time.
- Here, “service time” is not trivial because GPU kernels batch and because decode is incremental.

Pros
- In classic queueing, SRPT is near-optimal for mean response time and can strongly improve tail for short jobs.
- Automatically handles a spectrum (not just short/long buckets).

Cons / risks
- Prediction required; mispredictions are damaging.
- Known fairness issues: SRPT can starve large jobs without aging.
- Implementation complexity: we’d need a priority queue keyed by predicted cost, plus batching aware selection.
- “Remaining” time changes during decode; for streaming requests, we may keep a request “alive” for long time.

Prediction candidates
- predicted_prefill_cost_ms from (prompt_tokens, model, batch size) lookup table.
- predicted_total_tokens = prompt_tokens + max_new_tokens * expected_output_fraction.
- Use observed per-request prefill runtime to update an EWMA model (per route/model/hardware SKU) (but be careful about feedback loops).

Possible simplified SRPT variants
- Prefill-SRPT only: use SRPT ordering just for prefill admission into batches; keep decode scheduling mostly unchanged.
- Bucketed SRPT: multiple bins by predicted prefill cost (e.g., 0-20ms, 20-80ms, 80ms+), then do priority between bins.
- SRPT + aging: every X ms waiting reduces the effective predicted cost to prevent starvation.

Knobs
- aging_rate: how quickly large jobs “gain priority” while waiting.
- prediction caps: clamp predicted cost to [min,max] to avoid extreme decisions.

Cross-cutting dimension: per-phase scheduling (prefill vs decode)
Observation
- The worst p95 complaints tend to be “short requests stuck behind long prefills”.
- That suggests an approach focusing on prefill queueing may yield most gains with less risk.

Ideas
- Separate prefill queueing from decode queueing.
- Prioritize SHORT during prefill admission; once in decode, allow more mixing (decode is incremental and more naturally interleaves).
- But we must avoid cases where a single large prefill batch blocks the device long enough to hurt short latency anyway.

Parameter sketches / default starting points (NOT final)
Classification
- Short if prompt_tokens <= 256 (or predicted_prefill_ms <= 25ms)
- Long if prompt_tokens >= 1024 (or predicted_prefill_ms >= 80ms)
- Middle bucket treated as short initially (conservative for tail) OR treated as long (conservative for throughput) — needs data.

Two-queue fairness (Option C)
- max_long_wait_ms: 500ms (start; tighten later by tier)
- fairness_window_dispatches: 8 short dispatches then 1 long if long non-empty
- batch mixing rule (initial): do not mix long into short prefill batches; allow mixing within long batches.

WFQ/DRR (Option D)
- weights short:long = 4:1
- cost = prompt_tokens (v0), revisit with predicted_prefill_ms once we trust it
- add a hard max_long_wait_ms anyway as a safety valve

SRPT-like (Option E)
- bucketed SRPT on predicted_prefill_ms (3 buckets)
- aging: every 250ms waiting, promote one bucket up

Failure modes / gotchas to explicitly test
- Misclassification: a “short” that is actually expensive (e.g., due to special tokens, adapters, bad kernel path) hogs the short queue.
- Mixed streaming vs non-streaming: non-streaming long requests might tie up resources differently.
- Max_new_tokens abuse: short prompt but huge decode can still be a long job; classification must consider decode budgets.
- Priority inversion via batching: short request waits because it can’t form a batch while a long batch is being built/served.
- Burst oscillation: under periodic bursts of long prompts, scheduler flips and creates sawtooth queue depth.
- Overload: if we keep admitting short aggressively, long queue grows unbounded; need backpressure per class.

Benchmarks / how to decide
- Synthetic distributions:
  - 90% short / 10% long; 50/50; 10/90
  - bursty arrivals (on/off), long bursts, short bursts
  - varying max_new_tokens for short vs long
- Trace replays (representative customer mixes) — ask Rina/Jonas for canonical traces.
- Metrics to compare:
  - p95 short latency improvement target (relative)
  - throughput regression bound (absolute or %)
  - fairness: max long wait and long p99

My current recommendation (for prototype path)
- Implement Option C (two-queue + fairness window + max-long-wait guardrail) behind a flag.
- Keep classification simple (prompt_tokens threshold) but leave hooks for predicted_prefill_cost later.
- Add instrumentation early; don’t guess.

Open questions
1) What is the right unit for “fairness”? dispatches, tokens, or time?
2) Should “short” be defined by prompt_tokens only, or by predicted prefill ms (per model/hardware)?
3) Do we need a “medium” class or can we live with two buckets + guardrails?
4) How to handle decode-heavy requests with short prompt + huge max_new_tokens?
5) What batch mixing restrictions are actually necessary to avoid priority inversion?
6) Per-tier behavior: do we treat Dedicated interactive routes differently from bulk routes?

Next steps / action items (roll into Linear if we agree)
- Marcus: sanity-check implementation complexity for Option C vs DRR in current scheduler code.
- Omar/Julian: propose metric names and required histograms (per-class wait/service + starvation detector).
- Jonas/Rina: pick 3 benchmark scenarios that we’ll use to pick between Option C and DRR if needed.
- Sofia/Noah: agree on a single fairness guarantee statement we can put in the design doc (even if approximate).
